Content:
Remember that to solve a rational equation, such as the one below, we can use cross-multiplication:

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(x)|= (3)/(5); 5 ⋅ 2|= 3 ⋅ x; 10|= 3x; (10)/(3)|= x]

Content:
However, there is also another method that we can use, known as the flip method, which involves taking the reciprocal of both sides of an equation. So, when an equation involves two fractions, we can "flip" them as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc]

Content:
The above technique works whenever [MATH: a] and [MATH: c] are both different from zero.

Content:
The flip method is useful because it allows us to remove a variable from a denominator. For example, applying the flip method, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}x}=\dfrac{\color{blue}3}{\color{red}5} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\color{blue}x}{\color{red}2} = \dfrac{\color{red}5}{\color{blue}3}.]

Content:
Now, we can solve the resulting equation using the multiplication principle:

Content:
[MATH: 2 ⋅ (x)/(2)|= 2 ⋅ (5)/(3); 2 ⋅ (x)/(2)|= 2 ⋅ (5)/(3); x|= (10)/(3)]

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc]

The above technique works whenever [MATH: a] and [MATH: c] are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac 23 = \dfrac 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 32 = \dfrac x2]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we note that [MATH: x=-1] cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc]

The above technique works whenever [MATH: a] and [MATH: c] are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac 1{x+1} = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x+1}{1} = \dfrac 12]

The above equation simplifies to

[MATH: x+1 = \dfrac 12 .]

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

[MATH: x + 1|= (1)/(2); x + 1 − 1|= (1)/(2) − 1; x|= − (1)/(2)]

  • [MATH: x=0] cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc]

The above technique works whenever [MATH: a] and [MATH: c] are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac 1{x-2} = \dfrac 3{5x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x-2}{1} = \dfrac{5x}{3}]

The above equation simplifies to

[MATH: x-2 = \dfrac{5x}{3}.]

We can now solve this equation with the addition and multiplication principles: [MATH: 3 ⋅ (x − 2)|= 3 ⋅ (5x)/(3); 3x − 6|= 5x; 3x − 5x|= 6; − 2x|= 6; x|= − 3]
